# My question and data

I want to predict annual rainfall at the supplied grid locations for **each
year from 1970 to 1982**. I also want to show how uncertain those predictions
are. I fit each year separately: I do not treat repeated measurements at the
same station in different years as independent spatial locations.

My main idea is simple. Elevation and location describe the broad rainfall
pattern. Kriging then uses the similarity between nearby residuals to adjust
that pattern. Maximum likelihood estimates the model parameters, while
cross-validation helps me choose the model. This differs from IDW, which uses
distance weights without fitting a probability model for the rainfall field.

## Data checks and the matching grid

```{r load-data}
rain_file <- new.env()
invisible(load("data/RainData.RData", envir = rain_file))
rain <- rain_file$dati
grid <- rain_file$grid
years <- sort(unique(rain$anno))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(grid,
  rbind(rain_file$Basquota32, rain_file$Calabriaquota32),
  check.attributes = FALSE)))

# I correct the labels without removing any station or changing rainfall.
region_fix <- c("4085" = "Basilicata", "4086" = "Basilicata",
                "4367" = "Calabria")
rain$Nome_Regione <- as.character(rain$Nome_Regione)
fix_rows <- rain$ID %in% as.numeric(names(region_fix))
rain$Nome_Regione[fix_rows] <-
  unname(region_fix[as.character(rain$ID[fix_rows])])
stopifnot(identical(rain$totanno, rain_file$dati$totanno),
          nrow(rain) == nrow(rain_file$dati),
          !any(rain$Nome_Regione == "Puglia"))

fields <- c("ID", "anno", "XUTM", "YUTM", "Quota", "totanno")
stopifnot(!anyNA(rain[fields]), !anyNA(grid), all(rain$totanno > 0),
          !anyDuplicated(grid[c("XUTM", "YUTM")]))
for (yr in years) {
  d <- subset(rain, anno == yr)
  stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(d$ID),
            !anyDuplicated(d[c("XUTM", "YUTM")]))
}

# These fixed changes of units also apply to every validation fold.
add_coordinates <- function(d) {
  d$x <- d$XUTM / 1000
  d$y <- d$YUTM / 1000
  d$east <- (d$x - 1100) / 100
  d$north <- (d$y - 4400) / 100
  d$elev <- d$Quota / 1000
  d
}
rain <- add_coordinates(rain)
grid <- add_coordinates(grid)
rain$rain <- rain$totanno
annual <- split(rain, rain$anno)

data_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(annual, function(d) {
  data.frame(Year = d$anno[1], Stations = nrow(d),
    Mean_mm = mean(d$rain), SD_mm = sd(d$rain),
    Min_mm = min(d$rain), Max_mm = max(d$rain),
    Cor_elevation = cor(d$rain, d$Quota))
}))
knitr::kable(data_summary, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

There are **`r nrow(rain)` annual observations**, with no missing values in
the variables used here. All three corrected stations remain in the data.
The matching land grid has **`r nrow(grid)` points** and an elevation at
each point. It is already inside `RainData.RData`. The separately supplied
`AllGrids.RData` belongs to a marine dataset from other years, so I do not
use it for rainfall.

As in Homework 2, I interpret rainfall as **mm**, elevation as **m**, and
the supplied projected coordinates as **m**. These units are assumptions
based on the names and values; the files do not contain complete metadata.
I divide coordinates by 1,000 for distances in km and keep their common
projected system. I do not assign an unverified EPSG code. The extra centring
and scaling in `east`, `north` and `elev` help numerical fitting; distances
still use `x` and `y` in km.

Elevation is the environmental descriptor available at **both** stations
and grid points. Latitude and longitude repeat location information, and
the grid has no supplied regional factor. I therefore use elevation and
the projected coordinates as model covariates. I use the corrected regions
to describe the stations, not as an extra predictor.

## Where are the stations?

```{r map-tools}
draw_outlines <- function() {
  lines(rain_file$Bas$XUTM/1000, rain_file$Bas$YUTM/1000,
        col = "grey45", lwd = 0.7)
  lines(rain_file$Cal$XUTM/1000, rain_file$Cal$YUTM/1000,
        col = "grey45", lwd = 0.7)
}
map_frame <- function(title) {
  plot(grid$x, grid$y, type = "n", asp = 1,
    xlim = range(c(grid$x, rain$x)), ylim = range(c(grid$y, rain$y)),
    xlab = "Easting (km)", ylab = "Northing (km)", main = title)
  draw_outlines()
}
region_col <- c(Basilicata = "#377EB8", Calabria = "#E69F00")
```

```{r station-overview, fig.width=9, fig.height=5.6}
stations <- rain[!duplicated(rain$ID), ]
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
map_frame("Station locations")
points(stations$x, stations$y, pch = 19, cex = 0.55,
       col = region_col[stations$Nome_Regione])
i <- match(as.numeric(names(region_fix)), stations$ID)
points(stations$x[i], stations$y[i], pch = 1, cex = 1.5)
text(stations$x[i], stations$y[i], stations$ID[i],
     pos = c(2, 4, 2), cex = 0.65)
legend("bottomleft", names(region_col), col = region_col,
       pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.7)
map_frame("Supplied prediction grid")
points(grid$x, grid$y, pch = 15, cex = 0.35, col = "#267A8A")
points(stations$x, stations$y, pch = 1, cex = 0.3)
legend("bottomleft", c("Grid", "Stations"), pch = c(15, 1),
       col = c("#267A8A", "black"), bty = "n", cex = 0.7)
```

The stations are unevenly spaced along an elongated region. I expect
different prediction uncertainty in dense and sparse parts of this region.
The number of available stations changes by year, so I use that year's
locations when checking the support of each prediction map.

# Exploratory analysis before fitting

```{r rainfall-by-year, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.4}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(rain ~ anno, data = rain, las = 2, col = "#B9DCE5",
        xlab = "Year", ylab = "Rainfall (mm)", main = "Annual distributions")
plot(data_summary$Year, data_summary$Cor_elevation, type = "b",
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Year", ylab = "Correlation",
     main = "Rainfall and elevation", pch = 19, col = "#216681")
abline(h = 0, col = "grey70")
```

Rainfall and elevation have a positive association in every year: the
correlations range from **`r fmt(min(data_summary$Cor_elevation), 2)`** to
**`r fmt(max(data_summary$Cor_elevation), 2)`**. This supports including
elevation, but does not show a causal effect or explain all local variation.
The annual boxplots also show that the rainfall distribution changes with
the year. The highest observed station average is in
**`r data_summary$Year[which.max(data_summary$Mean_mm)]`**
(**`r fmt(max(data_summary$Mean_mm))` mm**), and the lowest is in
**`r data_summary$Year[which.min(data_summary$Mean_mm)]`**
(**`r fmt(min(data_summary$Mean_mm))` mm**).
Changes in station coverage mean that these averages are not
area-weighted regional rainfall totals or a formal time-trend analysis.

```{r covariate-plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
par(mfrow = c(4, 4), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 0.5), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0))
for (d in annual) {
  plot(d$Quota, d$rain, pch = 19, cex = 0.4, col = "#267A8A",
       xlab = "Elevation (m)", ylab = "Rainfall (mm)",
       main = as.character(d$anno[1]))
  lines(lowess(d$Quota, d$rain), col = "#C45A33", lwd = 1.5)
}
```

The smooth lines help me see the association without assuming it is exactly
linear. I use a linear elevation term as an understandable starting model,
and also consider a broad east–north trend. I do not add many polynomial
terms just to improve an in-sample fit.

## Distribution, trend and transformation

```{r distribution-checks}
skewness <- function(z) mean((z-mean(z))^3) / mean((z-mean(z))^2)^1.5
distribution_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(annual, function(d) {
  raw_res <- resid(lm(rain ~ elev + east + north, data = d))
  log_res <- resid(lm(log(rain) ~ elev + east + north, data = d))
  data.frame(Year = d$anno[1], Raw_skew = skewness(d$rain),
    Raw_residual_skew = skewness(raw_res),
    Log_residual_skew = skewness(log_res))
}))
knitr::kable(distribution_check, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The rainfall distributions are right-skewed. Removing a trend changes the
distribution, and using log rainfall often helps, but not in every year.
Skewness alone cannot establish Gaussianity. I therefore compare **raw and
log rainfall models** using held-out predictions on the same mm scale, and
show Q–Q diagnostics for the chosen models later. For a log model, the
transformation is used in fitting, variograms, prediction and intervals;
I return to mm only with the appropriate back-transformation.

# Choosing and fitting the models

## What the models mean

For each year I use the spatial model

\[
T\{Y(s)\}=X(s)\beta+w(s)+\epsilon(s).
\]

Here, $Y(s)$ is annual rainfall and $T$ is either the identity or the
natural logarithm. The trend $X(s)\beta$ describes the broad pattern.
The zero-mean process $w(s)$ describes remaining spatial variation, and
$\epsilon(s)$ has variance $\tau^2$, the nugget. I assume the two components
are independent. The residual covariance is stationary and isotropic:
it depends on distance, not on the absolute position or direction.

I compare two trends: **elevation**, and **elevation plus east and north
coordinates**. For each trend and response scale, I compare exponential,
spherical and Matérn covariance with fixed $\kappa=1.5$. This gives
**12 candidates per year**. The exponential allows a rougher field; the
spherical reaches zero correlation at a finite distance; Matérn 1.5 allows
a smoother field. Matérn 0.5 would repeat the exponential, so I do not add it
as a separate candidate.

All fits use **maximum likelihood**, not REML or Bayesian estimation.
For each candidate, I look for the parameter values that make the observed
spatial data most plausible under that model.
The semivariogram for nonzero distance is
$\gamma(h)=\tau^2+\sigma^2\{1-\rho(h)\}$, where $\sigma^2$ is the partial
sill. The total sill is $\tau^2+\sigma^2$. I estimate the nugget rather than
forcing the model to pass through every measured value.

```{r candidates}
trends <- list(Elevation = ~elev,
               Elevation_xy = ~elev + east + north)
candidates <- expand.grid(
  Scale = c("Raw", "Log"), Trend = names(trends),
  Covariance = c("exponential", "spherical", "matern"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
candidates$Model <- seq_len(nrow(candidates))
knitr::kable(candidates[c("Model", "Scale", "Trend", "Covariance")],
             row.names = FALSE)
```

## How I compare predictions

I use **five-fold cross-validation within each year**. All candidates use
the same split for that year. Each fit uses only the training stations;
the held-out rainfall values are used only to score predictions. The
random seeds are fixed, and no year contributes observations to another
year's model.

Because this homework asks for uncertainty intervals as well as a map,
my primary criterion is the **95% interval score**, averaged over all
held-out stations:

\[
IS_{0.05}=(u-l)+40(l-y)\,1(y<l)+40(y-u)\,1(y>u).
\]

This is a proper score for the central 95% interval. It penalises intervals
that are too wide and intervals that miss the observation. Lower is better.
Coverage and average width help explain the score, but coverage by itself
is not a proper score: a very wide interval could cover almost everything.
I select the lowest mean interval score. I also report **RMSE in mm** for
the predictive mean, calculated from all held-out errors together. Squared
error is a proper score for a predictive mean, and RMSE has the same ranking
as mean squared error. RMSE breaks an exact interval-score tie. This makes
interval quality the main objective, while still showing the cost in mean
prediction accuracy. I do not change the selection rule between years.

This distinction matters here: a raw Gaussian model can have a slightly
smaller RMSE while giving negative lower limits for rainfall. I compare
both scales, but I do not treat a tiny RMSE gain as enough evidence of
better uncertainty estimates.

These are **model-selection scores**. The best score can be optimistic
because I use it to choose among 12 candidates. Unlike the separate nested
assessment in Homework 3, I do not claim that this table is an independent
assessment of the complete selection procedure. Random folds mainly assess
interpolation among existing stations, not prediction across a large
unsampled region. A spatially separated outer validation would answer a
harder question.

## Reusable fitting and prediction functions

I repeat each likelihood fit from two starting range values and keep the
converged fit with the higher likelihood. This reduces dependence on a
single starting value, although it cannot prove a global maximum. Failed
starts are counted; if neither start converges, the analysis stops rather
than silently removing a model or station. I also inspect boundary estimates.

```{r model-functions}
design <- function(d, trend) {
  geoR::trend.spatial(trends[[trend]], d)
}

fit_one <- function(d, candidate) {
  z <- if (candidate$Scale == "Log") log(d$rain) else d$rain
  g <- geoR::as.geodata(data.frame(x = d$x, y = d$y, z = z,
    elev = d$elev, east = d$east, north = d$north), covar.col = 4:6)
  X <- design(d, candidate$Trend)
  s2 <- mean(lm.fit(X, z)$residuals^2)
  fits <- lapply(c(20, 80), function(start) {
    tryCatch(geoR::likfit(g, trend = trends[[candidate$Trend]],
      cov.model = candidate$Covariance, kappa = 1.5, fix.kappa = TRUE,
      ini.cov.pars = c(0.8*s2, start), nugget = 0.2*s2,
      fix.nugget = FALSE, lambda = 1, fix.lambda = TRUE,
      lik.method = "ML", limits = geoR::pars.limits(phi = c(0.5, 1500)),
      messages = FALSE, control = list(maxit = 2000)),
      error = function(e) NULL)
  })
  ok <- vapply(fits, function(m) {
    !is.null(m) && is.finite(m$loglik) &&
      m$info.minimisation.function$convergence == 0
  }, logical(1))
  if (!any(ok)) stop("No converged fit for this candidate.")
  valid <- fits[ok]
  fit <- valid[[which.max(vapply(valid, function(m) m$loglik, numeric(1)))]]
  list(fit = fit, g = g, X = X, rejected = sum(!ok))
}

predict_one <- function(f, locations, candidate) {
  p <- geoR::krige.conv(f$g,
    locations = as.matrix(locations[c("x", "y")]),
    krige = geoR::krige.control(type.krige = "OK", obj.model = f$fit,
      trend.d = f$X, trend.l = design(locations, candidate$Trend),
      micro.scale = 0),
    output = geoR::output.control(signal = FALSE, messages = FALSE))
  mu <- p$predict
  v <- p$krige.var
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(mu)), all(is.finite(v)), all(v > 0))
  lower <- mu - qnorm(0.975)*sqrt(v)
  upper <- mu + qnorm(0.975)*sqrt(v)
  if (candidate$Scale == "Log") {
    answer <- data.frame(Mean = exp(mu + v/2),
                         Lower = exp(lower), Upper = exp(upper))
  } else {
    answer <- data.frame(Mean = mu, Lower = lower, Upper = upper)
  }
  answer$mu <- mu
  answer$variance <- v
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(answer))))
  answer
}

score_predictions <- function(y, p) {
  interval_score <- (p$Upper-p$Lower) +
    40*pmax(p$Lower-y, 0) + 40*pmax(y-p$Upper, 0)
  data.frame(RMSE = sqrt(mean((p$Mean-y)^2)),
    IS95 = mean(interval_score),
    Coverage = 100*mean(y >= p$Lower & y <= p$Upper),
    Width = mean(p$Upper-p$Lower), Bias = mean(p$Mean-y))
}
```

The `OK` option in `geoR` estimates the trend coefficients. With the
external elevation and coordinate design matrices above, the prediction is
**universal kriging**, despite that option name. I explicitly use
`signal = FALSE` to predict an annual observation, including the nugget.

## Pointwise intervals and the log scale

For a raw Gaussian model, the predictive mean is $m$ and the interval is
$m\pm1.96\sqrt{v}$. For a log model, $m$ and $v$ refer to log rainfall.
On the original scale I use

\[
\widehat{E(Y\mid\text{data})}=\exp(m+v/2),\qquad
[l,u]=[\exp(m-1.96\sqrt v),\ \exp(m+1.96\sqrt v)].
\]

Simply using $\exp(m)$ would give the predictive median, not the mean
needed for squared-error comparison. I apply the same formulas in
cross-validation and on the grid. I log the data explicitly and keep
`lambda = 1` in `geoR` to avoid applying the transformation twice.

For the homework's pointwise confidence intervals, I report **approximate
95% prediction intervals for unknown annual rainfall at each location**.
They include spatial uncertainty, the nugget and the universal-kriging
correction for estimating the mean coefficients. They treat the fitted
covariance parameters and selected model as fixed, so they do not include
their uncertainty. They are not confidence intervals for a regression
coefficient, Bayesian credible intervals, or a simultaneous 95% band for
all grid points. Intervals for only the smooth latent signal would be
narrower because they would exclude the new observation's nugget.

```{r yearly-function}
analyse_year <- function(d, grid) {
  set.seed(2026 + d$anno[1])
  fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(d)))
  predictions <- vector("list", nrow(candidates))
  scores <- vector("list", nrow(candidates))
  rejected <- integer(nrow(candidates))
  for (j in seq_len(nrow(candidates))) {
    p <- data.frame(Mean = rep(NA_real_, nrow(d)), Lower = NA_real_,
                    Upper = NA_real_, mu = NA_real_, variance = NA_real_)
    for (k in 1:5) {
      test <- fold == k
      f <- fit_one(d[!test, ], candidates[j, ])
      p[test, ] <- predict_one(f, d[test, ], candidates[j, ])
      rejected[j] <- rejected[j] + f$rejected
    }
    predictions[[j]] <- p
    scores[[j]] <- score_predictions(d$rain, p)
  }
  scores <- cbind(candidates, do.call(rbind, scores))
  ranking <- order(scores$IS95, scores$RMSE)
  best <- ranking[1]
  fitted <- fit_one(d, candidates[best, ])
  mapped <- predict_one(fitted, grid, candidates[best, ])
  hull <- chull(d$x, d$y)
  mapped$Outside_hull <- sp::point.in.polygon(
    grid$x, grid$y, d$x[hull], d$y[hull]) == 0
  mapped$Outside_elevation <- grid$Quota < min(d$Quota) |
                              grid$Quota > max(d$Quota)
  list(year = d$anno[1], fold = fold, scores = scores,
    predictions = predictions, best = best, runner_up = ranking[2],
    fitted = fitted, mapped = mapped,
    rejected = sum(rejected) + fitted$rejected)
}
```

```{r fit-all-years, cache=TRUE, cache.vars="results", cache.extra=list(tools::md5sum("data/RainData.RData"), candidates, lapply(trends, deparse), lapply(list(add_coordinates, design, fit_one, predict_one, score_predictions, analyse_year), deparse), as.character(packageVersion("geoR")))}
# I repeat the same independent yearly analysis; seeds are set inside it.
if (.Platform$OS.type == "unix") {
  results <- parallel::mclapply(annual, analyse_year, grid = grid,
    mc.cores = 4, mc.set.seed = FALSE)
} else {
  results <- lapply(annual, analyse_year, grid = grid)
}
stopifnot(!any(vapply(results, inherits, logical(1), "try-error")))
```

# Results and model choices

```{r selection-summary}
selected <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results, function(r) {
  a <- r$scores[r$best, ]
  data.frame(Year = r$year, Model = a$Model, Scale = a$Scale,
    Trend = a$Trend, Covariance = a$Covariance, IS95_mm = a$IS95,
    RMSE_mm = a$RMSE)
}))
knitr::kable(selected, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The selected model has the smallest mean interval score **among these
candidates on this split**. It is not a uniquely established model. The
complete candidate scores are in the appendix, so the choice can be checked
rather than taken on trust. Small differences between candidates should
not receive a strong scientific interpretation.

I select log models in **`r sum(selected$Scale == "Log")` of
`r length(years)` years**, and the elevation-plus-coordinate trend in
**`r sum(selected$Trend == "Elevation_xy")` years**. The choices can
change with the validation split or the candidate list. The winning
interval-score models use the log scale in every year; this is a result
of the comparison, not a requirement imposed on the candidates.

```{r uncertainty-scores}
interval_results <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results, function(r) {
  a <- r$scores[r$best, ]
  data.frame(Year = r$year, IS95_mm = a$IS95,
    Coverage_percent = a$Coverage, Width_mm = a$Width, Bias_mm = a$Bias,
    RMSE_cost_mm = a$RMSE - min(r$scores$RMSE))
}))
knitr::kable(interval_results, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

The selected models have coverage between
**`r fmt(min(interval_results$Coverage_percent))`%** and
**`r fmt(max(interval_results$Coverage_percent))`%**, compared with the
nominal 95%. The weakest coverage is in
**`r interval_results$Year[which.min(interval_results$Coverage_percent)]`**,
so choosing by interval score does not make the intervals perfectly
calibrated. Positive bias means overprediction. `RMSE_cost_mm` is the
extra RMSE compared with the best mean-prediction candidate. Its maximum
is **`r fmt(max(interval_results$RMSE_cost_mm), 2)` mm**. This makes the
trade-off visible instead of claiming one model is best for every purpose.
These diagnostics also use the selection folds, so I do not describe them
as independent guarantees of coverage.

```{r score-tradeoff-example}
example <- results[["1981"]]
point_best <- which.min(example$scores$RMSE)
point_score <- example$scores[point_best, ]
interval_score <- example$scores[example$best, ]
negative_limits <- sum(example$predictions[[point_best]]$Lower < 0)
```

For example, in 1981 the raw model's RMSE is
**`r fmt(point_score$RMSE, 2)` mm**, compared with
**`r fmt(interval_score$RMSE, 2)` mm** for the selected log model.
However, its interval score is **`r fmt(point_score$IS95, 2)` mm**, compared
with **`r fmt(interval_score$IS95, 2)` mm** for the log model. The raw model
also gives negative lower limits at **`r negative_limits` held-out stations**.
Here I accept a small increase in RMSE for better interval predictions and
a distribution that respects the positive rainfall scale.

## Fitted covariance parameters

```{r parameter-summary}
parameters <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results, function(r) {
  m <- r$fitted$fit
  data.frame(Year = r$year, Partial_sill = m$cov.pars[1],
    Nugget = m$nugget, Nugget_share = m$nugget/sum(m$cov.pars[1], m$nugget),
    Phi_km = m$cov.pars[2],
    Range_bound = m$cov.pars[2] < 0.51 | m$cov.pars[2] > 1499,
    Rejected_starts = r$rejected)
}))
knitr::kable(parameters, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

All selected models use log rainfall, so the variance parameters in this
table are in **squared log units**. The distance units are unchanged.
`Phi_km` is the software's range parameter: it is the exact
range for the spherical model, while an exponential correlation falls to
about 0.05 at $3\phi$. For Matérn 1.5, that distance is about
$4.74\phi$. I therefore interpret the range using the selected family.

I balance trend fit with residual structure. A smaller nugget is not a
selection rule by itself, and a larger nugget does not automatically mean
bad measurements. Boundary estimates and noisy diagnostic curves make
precise parameter interpretations less reliable. There are
**`r sum(parameters$Range_bound)` selected fits at a range bound** and
**`r sum(parameters$Rejected_starts)` rejected starts** across the fitting
and validation runs. Every candidate still has a converged fit in every fold.

# Diagnostics for the selected models

I examine the raw and detrended semivariograms on the **selected response
scale**. A rising raw curve can reflect a changing mean, not only residual
dependence. The fitted curve comes from maximum likelihood; it is not a
least-squares fit to the plotted variogram points. I use 12 bins up to half
the maximum station separation. The pair counts are retained with the
diagnostics because sparse bins are less stable.

```{r diagnostic-functions}
diagnostics <- lapply(results, function(r) {
  f <- r$fitted
  cnd <- candidates[r$best, ]
  cutoff <- max(dist(f$g$coords))/2
  breaks <- seq(0, cutoff, length.out = 13)
  raw <- geoR::variog(f$g, breaks = breaks, trend = "cte",
                      messages = FALSE)
  adjusted <- geoR::variog(f$g, breaks = breaks,
    trend = trends[[cnd$Trend]], messages = FALSE)
  dirs <- lapply(c(0, 45, 90, 135), function(a) {
    geoR::variog(f$g, breaks = breaks, trend = trends[[cnd$Trend]],
      direction = a*pi/180, tolerance = pi/8, messages = FALSE)
  })
  list(raw = raw, adjusted = adjusted, directions = dirs)
})
```

```{r yearly-diagnostics, fig.width=10, fig.height=7.5, results='asis'}
groups <- split(seq_along(results),
                cut(seq_along(results), breaks = 4, labels = FALSE))
for (indices in groups) {
  par(mfrow = c(length(indices), 3), mar = c(3, 3, 2, 0.5),
      mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0))
  for (i in indices) {
    r <- results[[i]]
    dg <- diagnostics[[i]]
    m <- r$fitted$fit
    cnd <- candidates[r$best, ]
    d <- annual[[i]]
    p <- r$predictions[[r$best]]
    z <- if (cnd$Scale == "Log") log(d$rain) else d$rain
    qqnorm((z-p$mu)/sqrt(p$variance), pch = 19, cex = 0.35,
      main = paste(r$year, "held-out Q-Q"), xlab = "Normal quantile",
      ylab = "Standardised error")
    abline(0, 1, col = "#C45A33")
    h <- seq(0, max(dg$raw$u), length.out = 100)
    curve <- m$nugget + m$cov.pars[1] -
      geoR::cov.spatial(h, cov.model = m$cov.model,
                        cov.pars = m$cov.pars, kappa = m$kappa)
    plot(dg$raw$u, dg$raw$v, type = "b", pch = 1, cex = 0.45,
      ylim = range(c(dg$raw$v, dg$adjusted$v, curve)),
      main = paste(r$year, "variograms"), xlab = "Distance (km)",
      ylab = "Semivariance")
    lines(dg$adjusted$u, dg$adjusted$v, type = "b", pch = 19,
          cex = 0.45, col = "#267A8A")
    lines(h, curve, col = "#C45A33", lwd = 1.5)
    if (i == indices[1]) legend("topleft", c("Raw", "Detrended", "ML"),
      col = c("black", "#267A8A", "#C45A33"), lty = 1,
      cex = 0.75, bty = "n")
    plot(dg$adjusted$u, dg$adjusted$v, type = "n",
      ylim = range(unlist(lapply(dg$directions, function(v) v$v))),
      main = paste(r$year, "directions"), xlab = "Distance (km)",
      ylab = "Residual semivariance")
    for (k in 1:4) lines(dg$directions[[k]]$u, dg$directions[[k]]$v,
                        col = k, lty = k)
    if (i == indices[1]) legend("topleft", c("0", "45", "90", "135"),
                          col = 1:4, lty = 1:4, cex = 0.75, bty = "n")
  }
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

The Q–Q plots assess held-out errors on the model scale, including their
predicted standard deviations. Tail departures warn me that Gaussian
intervals may be imperfect. These errors share training observations, so
they are not independent observations for a formal normality test.
The directional variograms (angles in degrees) help check the isotropy
assumption. Differences
can also arise from unequal pair counts, the elongated sampling region,
or a trend that is too simple. The plots do not prove stationarity or
isotropy. In particular, the lower tails in 1980 and 1982 depart from
the normal line. I keep those observations, but unusual dry locations may
be harder to predict than the Gaussian approximation suggests. The
directional curves also differ at longer distances, so isotropy remains
a working approximation. I keep these limits explicit when interpreting
the maps.

```{r pair-counts}
pair_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(results), function(i) {
  dg <- diagnostics[[i]]
  data.frame(Year = results[[i]]$year,
    Min_pairs = min(dg$adjusted$n), Max_pairs = max(dg$adjusted$n),
    Min_directional_pairs = min(unlist(lapply(dg$directions,
                                             function(v) v$n))))
}))
knitr::kable(pair_check, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Rainfall maps and pointwise intervals

Each yearly page shows the predicted **mean annual observation**, the
lower and upper 95% limits, and the interval width. The first three maps
share a colour scale within that year, so their colours are directly
comparable. The width map has its own scale. Scales are printed on every
page and may change between years. I keep the supplied 1,005 grid points;
I do not fill in a different regular grid.

Small black dots are that year's observed stations. A cross marks a grid
point outside the station convex hull, and an open triangle marks an
elevation outside the range observed that year. I keep these points, but
their predictions depend more strongly on model extrapolation. Neither
flag captures every possible form of extrapolation.

```{r grid-summary}
map_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results, function(r) {
  p <- r$mapped
  data.frame(Year = r$year, Min_mean = min(p$Mean), Max_mean = max(p$Mean),
    Median_width = median(p$Upper-p$Lower),
    Outside_hull = sum(p$Outside_hull),
    Outside_elevation = sum(p$Outside_elevation),
    Negative_lower = sum(p$Lower < 0))
}))
knitr::kable(map_summary, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

The grid elevations range from **`r min(grid$Quota)` to
`r max(grid$Quota)` m**, while station elevations across all years range
from **`r min(rain$Quota)` to `r max(rain$Quota)` m**. Predictions high in
the mountains therefore extend beyond the elevation information in the
data. A wide interval is useful evidence of uncertainty, but it may still
understate uncertainty from extrapolating an incorrect trend.
All the selected models use log rainfall, so their lower limits stay
positive. The raw Gaussian candidates can produce negative lower limits,
as the 1981 validation example shows. I do not repair such limits by
silently truncating them, because that would change the stated model.

For a log model, a large interval width in mm can reflect both uncertainty
on the log scale and a high rainfall level. Even the same log-scale standard
error gives a wider interval in mm at a wetter location. I therefore do not
read the width map as a map of station density alone.

```{r map-function}
draw_values <- function(values, breaks, title, d, p) {
  colours <- hcl.colors(length(breaks)-1, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE)
  map_frame(title)
  index <- cut(values, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
  points(grid$x, grid$y, pch = 15, cex = 0.55, col = colours[index])
  draw_outlines()
  points(d$x, d$y, pch = 20, cex = 0.18)
  points(grid$x[p$Outside_hull], grid$y[p$Outside_hull],
         pch = 4, cex = 0.38, col = "grey25")
  points(grid$x[p$Outside_elevation], grid$y[p$Outside_elevation],
         pch = 2, cex = 0.48, col = "#B33A26")
  labels <- paste(head(breaks, -1), tail(breaks, -1), sep = " to ")
  legend("bottomleft", labels, fill = colours, title = "mm",
         bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
}
```

```{r yearly-maps, results='asis', fig.width=7.5, fig.height=8}
for (i in seq_along(results)) {
  r <- results[[i]]
  p <- r$mapped
  d <- annual[[i]]
  a <- r$scores[r$best, ]
  cat("\n\n\\newpage\n\n## Year ", r$year, "\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("I use model ", a$Model, ": ", a$Scale, ", ", a$Trend,
      ", ", a$Covariance, ". Selection interval score is ", fmt(a$IS95),
      " mm and RMSE is ", fmt(a$RMSE),
      " mm; held-out coverage is ", fmt(a$Coverage), "%. ",
      "Predicted means range from ", fmt(min(p$Mean)), " to ",
      fmt(max(p$Mean)), " mm. The median interval width is ",
      fmt(median(p$Upper-p$Lower)), " mm.\n\n", sep = "")
  breaks <- pretty(range(p[c("Mean", "Lower", "Upper")]), n = 6)
  width_breaks <- pretty(range(p$Upper-p$Lower), n = 6)
  par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.3, 0.5),
      mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
  draw_values(p$Mean, breaks, "Predicted mean", d, p)
  draw_values(p$Lower, breaks, "Lower 95% limit", d, p)
  draw_values(p$Upper, breaks, "Upper 95% limit", d, p)
  draw_values(p$Upper-p$Lower, width_breaks, "95% interval width", d, p)
  cat("\n\nCrosses: outside station hull. Red triangles: elevation ",
      "outside the observed range. ", sum(p$Outside_hull),
      " grid points are outside the hull and ", sum(p$Outside_elevation),
      " have an extrapolated elevation. These groups may overlap.\n\n",
      sep = "")
}
```

\newpage

# What I take from the results

Across the maps, higher predicted rainfall often follows the higher
elevations, with local variation added by the spatial residual correction.
This is consistent with the positive rainfall–elevation association seen
in the observations. It does not mean elevation explains every wet or dry
location.

The maps separate the estimated rainfall pattern from its uncertainty.
I should read the predicted mean together with the lower and upper limits,
especially near the boundary and at elevations beyond the station range.
A detailed-looking map is not evidence that every local feature is well known.

The best-scoring model is allowed to change by year. This does not mean
that the physical process suddenly changes covariance family each year:
finite samples, changing stations and small score differences can also
change the ranking. I use one common set of candidate models and one common
selection rule to make the yearly analysis consistent.

The important limits are the assumed trend and residual stationarity,
isotropy, Gaussian approximation on the selected scale, and treating the
estimated covariance parameters as known. The validation split also matters.
Repeating the splits or using spatially separated validation would help
assess stability, while a bootstrap or a Bayesian analysis could address
more parameter uncertainty. Those are extensions, not analyses performed here.

# Appendix: all candidate scores

The tables below make the selection rule checkable. `IS95` and `Width` are
in mm, `Coverage` is a percentage, and the Matérn model always has
$\kappa=1.5$. Rows are ordered by interval score. The first row is selected.

```{r full-score-tables, results='asis'}
for (r in results) {
  cat("\n\n### ", r$year, "\n\n", sep = "")
  tab <- r$scores[order(r$scores$IS95, r$scores$RMSE),
                 c("Model", "IS95", "RMSE", "Coverage", "Width")]
  print(knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE))
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

# Sources and reproducibility

I used the supplied course notes by Giovanna Jona Lasinio,
*Chapter1-2* (exploration, trend and variograms), *Chapter3-5* (Gaussian
spatial models, maximum likelihood and kriging uncertainty), and
*Chapter6-11*, Section 10.3 (predictive validation and interval score).
The last score applies to central prediction intervals here; I am not
using Bayesian estimation. I also checked the `geoR` definitions of
`likfit`, `trend.spatial`, `krige.control` and `krige.conv`, especially
external covariates, Matérn smoothness and the observation prediction target.

```{r package-versions}
packages <- c("geoR", "sp", "knitr", "rmarkdown")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Component = c("R", packages),
  Version = c(as.character(getRversion()),
    vapply(packages, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)),
           character(1)))), row.names = FALSE)
```

# Use of AI

I used ChatGPT/Codex to help develop the analysis plan, write and run the
R code, check the prediction and interval calculations, and draft the
comments in this report. AI assistance covered the data checks, yearly
model comparisons, likelihood fits, validation, maps and compilation.
I asked for simple code and explanations that I could follow and discuss
in class. The main request was to analyse every rainfall year using the
matching grid, choose trend and covariance models by predictive scores,
and report pointwise intervals with their assumptions. The computations
were run in the AI-assisted R environment. This report does not claim an
independent manual replication by me; I remain responsible for reviewing
the results and understanding the choices before presenting them.
